provenance: Copied from the Foundry IQ graph session's Phase 2 runtime contract (graph-evidence/runtime-contract, commit 09cf71d): curated questions, allowlisted GQL, notes and topic maps. Passage and blob keys are SHA-256 prefixes; index and storage names stay in the private binding. Source URLs were read from the public industry indexes.

retail.title: Retail: U.S. CPSC product recalls (public, English)

s08.question: Which recalls were announced jointly with Mexico's consumer protection agency (PROFECO), and which company recalled each product?
s08.why: The joint-recall flag sits in each notice's metadata; plain search returns at most five notices that mention Mexico, while one graph query returns all ten with their recalling companies, each cited.

gold.answer: Ten recalls, each also joint with Health Canada: 19136 (Hayward Industries), 19186 (Contigo), 19189 (Whirlpool), 19752 (Ningbo Singfun Electric Appliance; also Amazon), 21174 (New Widetech), 22089 (Fitbit), 22237 (Hyper Products), 23721 (LG Electronics), 25009 (Fisher-Price) and 25413 (Tegu).

statements.label: PROFECO ← joint recall → recalled by company
statements.gql: MATCH (g:`Regulator`)<-[:`jointWith`]-(r:`Recall`)-[:`recalledBy`]->(c:`Company`) WHERE LOWER(g.name) CONTAINS 'profeco' OR LOWER(g.name) CONTAINS 'mexico' RETURN DISTINCT r.name AS recall, c.name AS company ORDER BY recall LIMIT 30

s08.question: Which carbon-monoxide recalls were later expanded or re-announced, and which earlier recall does each link to?
s08.why: Each link is stated in only one notice's related-recall field; the graph turns those into edges, joins them to the carbon-monoxide hazard and returns both recall families in one query.

gold.answer: Two recall families: Generac's recall 26494 expands recall 22127, and ZLINE's gas-range recall 23083 was expanded by 23107 and again by 24028.

statements.label: Carbon-monoxide hazard ← recall ← linked (expanded or re-announced) recall
statements.gql: MATCH (h:`Hazard`)<-[:`recallHazard`]-(o:`Recall`)<-[:`expandsRecall`]-(r:`Recall`) WHERE LOWER(h.name) CONTAINS 'carbon monoxide' RETURN DISTINCT r.name AS linkedRecall, o.name AS carbonMonoxideRecall ORDER BY linkedRecall LIMIT 20

s08.question: Which recalled products were sold on Temu or Shein?
s08.why: The retailer is one line inside each notice; plain search returns five notices, while the graph's product → sold-at edges return all sixteen recalls and their products, each cited.

gold.answer: Sixteen recalls: 21769, 24211, 24265, 25131, 25166, 25172, 25233, 25474, 26148, 26244, 26524, 26536, 26654, 26694, 26779 and 26794. They range from children's sleepwear and bike helmets to magnet sets, high chairs, crib bumpers, dressers, youth ATVs, air purifiers, security cameras, dive sticks and pressure washers.

statements.label: Temu or Shein ← sold at ← product ← recall
statements.gql: MATCH (s:`Retailer`)<-[:`soldAt`]-(p:`Product`)<-[:`recallsProduct`]-(r:`Recall`) WHERE LOWER(s.name) CONTAINS 'temu' OR LOWER(s.name) CONTAINS 'shein' RETURN DISTINCT r.name AS recall, p.name AS product ORDER BY recall LIMIT 40

s08.question: The STURDY Act recalls were about button-battery ingestion. Which products were affected?
s08.why: Plain search returns dresser and battery passages side by side; the graph shows the STURDY recalls' hazards, proves no ingestion path exists and points to the rule that does cover batteries.

gold.answer: The premise is false. The STURDY Act sets tip-over standards for clothing storage units, and the recalls that cite it are dresser tip-over and entrapment recalls; none has an ingestion or battery hazard. Button- and coin-battery recalls cite Reese's Law instead.

statements.label: Premise check: hazards of recalls that cite the STURDY Act
statements.gql: MATCH (r:`Recall`)-[:`recallCitesRule`]->(u:`Rule`), (r)-[:`recallHazard`]->(h:`Hazard`) WHERE LOWER(u.name) CONTAINS 'sturdy' RETURN DISTINCT u.name AS rule, h.name AS hazard ORDER BY hazard LIMIT 20

statements.label: Any STURDY Act recall with an ingestion or battery hazard (expected: none)
statements.gql: MATCH (r:`Recall`)-[:`recallCitesRule`]->(u:`Rule`), (r)-[:`recallHazard`]->(h:`Hazard`) WHERE LOWER(u.name) CONTAINS 'sturdy' AND (LOWER(h.name) CONTAINS 'ingest' OR LOWER(h.name) CONTAINS 'battery') RETURN r.name AS recall, h.name AS hazard LIMIT 5

statements.label: Which rule button-battery recalls cite instead
statements.gql: MATCH (r:`Recall`)-[:`recallCitesRule`]->(u:`Rule`) WHERE LOWER(u.name) CONTAINS 'reese' RETURN DISTINCT u.name AS rule, r.name AS recall ORDER BY recall LIMIT 10

s09.question: What are the main themes across these product recalls, and how much of the collection does each cover?
s09.why: The Topic Graph answers the corpus-wide question with named themes and their share of passages; plain search can only return five passages and cannot measure coverage.

gold.answer: Children's products (about 11% of passages), home furniture (10%), heater fire and burn (9%), lithium-ion power banks (8%), infant sleep products (8%), outdoor power tools (7%), Electrolux and GE ranges (7%) and kitchen-appliance burns (6%), followed by smaller themes such as magnets, bike helmets, e-bikes and carbon-monoxide heating products.

s09.question: Break down the children's product recalls: which sub-themes are there and how large is each?
s09.why: The Topic Graph already knows how children's recalls split and in what proportion; plain search returns recall passages without grouping or measuring them.

gold.answer: About 11% of passages, split into water-bead squishy toys and lead-related children's products (about 3% each), tools and devices with button batteries and light-up toys with button batteries (about 2% each), and the Contigo kids' water bottle recall (about 1%).

s09.question: What topics come up in these CPSC recalls?
s09.why: Plain hybrid search returns four light-up-toy recalls and one infant-sleep recall (2 areas); topic-balanced retrieval spreads its five recalls across 5 areas.

gold.answer: Recalls span button-battery light-up toys, e-bike fires, a children's water bottle, water-bead toys and infant sleep products.

s09.question: What should parents know about recalled products?
s09.why: Plain hybrid search returns three wintergreen-oil recalls among its five (3 areas); topic-balanced retrieval spreads them across 5, adding kitchen burns and water beads.

gold.answer: Parents should know about button and coin batteries, kitchen-appliance burn hazards, lead in children's products, water-bead toys and wintergreen essential oils.

financial.title: Financial services: CFPB complaints and OCC/FDIC supervisory guidance (public, English)

s08.question: A customer says a wire transfer was sent to a scammer. Which rules govern wire transfers, and which consumer complaints describe wire-transfer problems?
s08.why: Complaints describe what went wrong and supervisory guidance says which rules govern wires, and no single document holds both; the graph joins them through the shared wire-transfer channel and cites both sides.

gold.answer: OCC and FDIC guidance ties wire transfers to Regulation J (12 CFR 210 subpart B, Fedwire), UCC Article 4A, BSA funds-transfer recordkeeping (31 CFR 103.33) and OFAC regulations. The graph joins those rules to CFPB complaints that describe wire transfers, for example complaints 19895083, 19931691 and 4776438.

statements.label: Rules that govern wire transfers and Fedwire
statements.gql: MATCH (r:`Regulation`)-[:`regulationGovernsChannel`]->(ch:`PaymentChannel`) WHERE LOWER(ch.name) CONTAINS 'wire' RETURN DISTINCT r.name AS rule, ch.name AS channel ORDER BY rule LIMIT 20

statements.label: Complaints joined to Regulation J through the shared wire-transfer channel
statements.gql: MATCH (c:`Complaint`)-[:`complaintUsesChannel`]->(ch:`PaymentChannel`)<-[:`regulationGovernsChannel`]-(r:`Regulation`) WHERE LOWER(ch.name) CONTAINS 'wire' AND r.name = 'Regulation J' RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS complaint, ch.name AS channel, r.name AS rule ORDER BY complaint LIMIT 12

s08.question: Which agency administers each rule our payments compliance team tracks: the Bank Secrecy Act, OFAC regulations, Regulation E, Regulation J and the USA PATRIOT Act?
s08.why: The five answers sit in four documents; plain search returns FDIC manual passages that never pair Regulation E or Regulation J with their agencies, while one graph query returns every rule → agency pair with its citation.

gold.answer: Bank Secrecy Act: FinCEN. OFAC regulations: OFAC. Regulation E: CFPB. Regulation J: the Federal Reserve Board of Governors. USA PATRIOT Act: Treasury.

statements.label: Rule → administered by agency
statements.gql: MATCH (r:`Regulation`)-[:`regulationAdministeredBy`]->(x:`Regulator`) WHERE r.name IN ['Regulation E', 'Regulation J', 'Bank Secrecy Act', 'BSA', 'OFAC regulations', 'USA PATRIOT Act'] RETURN DISTINCT r.name AS rule, x.name AS administeredBy ORDER BY rule LIMIT 30

s08.question: Which complaints about government benefit cards (such as state unemployment debit cards) ended with monetary relief?
s08.why: Plain search finds benefit-card complaints but mixes in one that got only non-monetary relief and misses one that was refunded, and the reader must open each to check the outcome; the graph returns all ten with their outcomes, five of them monetary relief.

gold.answer: Ten complaints involve government benefit cards. Five were closed with monetary relief: 4421546, 4444894, 4523529, 4848417 and 5144422. One (4396385) got non-monetary relief and four were closed with an explanation.

statements.label: Government benefit card ← complaint → how the company closed it
statements.gql: MATCH (p:`FinancialProduct`)<-[:`complaintAboutProduct`]-(c:`Complaint`)-[:`complaintResolution`]->(res:`Resolution`) WHERE LOWER(p.name) CONTAINS 'government benefit' RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS complaint, res.name AS resolution ORDER BY resolution, complaint LIMIT 40

s08.question: Regulation E covers wire transfers, so which Regulation E error-resolution rights apply to a disputed wire?
s08.why: Plain search returns Regulation E passages that look relevant to any electronic payment; the graph shows what Regulation E actually governs, proves no Regulation E → wire link exists and names the rules that do govern wires.

gold.answer: The premise does not hold in these sources. The guidance ties Regulation E and the EFTA to electronic fund transfers and to payment, prepaid and reloadable cards, and the graph has no Regulation E → wire-transfer link. Wire transfers are governed by Regulation J (Fedwire) and UCC Article 4A. (Regulation E's separate remittance-transfer rules, which can reach some consumer international transfers, are not part of this path.)

statements.label: Premise check: what Regulation E and the EFTA govern
statements.gql: MATCH (r:`Regulation`)-[:`regulationGovernsChannel`]->(ch:`PaymentChannel`) WHERE LOWER(r.name) CONTAINS 'regulation e' OR LOWER(r.name) CONTAINS 'electronic fund transfer' OR r.name = 'EFTA' RETURN DISTINCT r.name AS regulation, ch.name AS governs ORDER BY governs LIMIT 20

statements.label: Any Regulation E → wire-transfer link (expected: none)
statements.gql: MATCH (r:`Regulation`)-[:`regulationGovernsChannel`]->(ch:`PaymentChannel`) WHERE (LOWER(r.name) CONTAINS 'regulation e' OR LOWER(r.name) CONTAINS 'electronic fund transfer') AND LOWER(ch.name) CONTAINS 'wire' RETURN r.name AS regulation, ch.name AS channel LIMIT 5

statements.label: What does govern wire transfers
statements.gql: MATCH (r:`Regulation`)-[:`regulationGovernsChannel`]->(ch:`PaymentChannel`) WHERE (LOWER(ch.name) CONTAINS 'wire') AND (LOWER(r.name) CONTAINS 'article 4a' OR LOWER(r.name) CONTAINS 'regulation j') RETURN DISTINCT r.name AS rule, ch.name AS channel ORDER BY rule LIMIT 10

s09.question: What are the main themes across these banking complaints and supervisory documents, and how much of the collection does each cover?
s09.why: The Topic Graph answers the corpus-wide question with named themes and their share of passages; plain search can only return five passages and cannot measure coverage.

gold.answer: Two halves. Supervisory guidance: payment-systems risk (about 12% of passages), liquidity (12%), trade finance (11%), BSA, CIP and enhanced due diligence (11%), three capital themes (about 19% together), counterparty credit risk (4%) and funds-transfer credit controls (2%). Consumer complaints: fraudulent wires and account holds (11%), checking accounts (9%) and money transfers and wallets (8%).

s09.question: Break down the complaints about fraudulent wires and account holds: which sub-themes are there and how large is each?
s09.why: The Topic Graph already knows how these complaints split and in what proportion; plain search returns complaint passages without grouping or measuring them.
s09.focusTopic: Fraudulent Wires, Credit, and Account Holds

gold.answer: About 11% of passages, split into unauthorized fraud with poor investigation (about 3%), wire-transfer disputes and delays (3%), unauthorized wires and fraud handling (2%), bank fraud-scam victim cases (2%) and account blocks and frozen funds (1%).

s09.question: What do regulators expect from banks?
s09.why: Plain hybrid search draws all five passages from 3 capital areas; topic-balanced retrieval spreads them across 5, adding BSA funds-transfer monitoring, funds-transfer credit controls and payment-systems risk.

gold.answer: Regulators expect adequate capital, monitoring of suspicious funds transfers under the BSA, credit controls on funds transfers and sound payment-systems risk management.

s09.question: What do consumers complain about to the CFPB?
s09.why: Plain hybrid search draws its five complaints from 3 areas; topic-balanced retrieval spreads them across 5, adding money-transfer fraud and EFT disputes.

gold.answer: Consumers complain about checking-account management, credit and benefit-card problems, money-transfer fraud and credit-union account and EFT disputes.

healthcare.title: Healthcare: FDA drug labels and ICD-10-CM coding guidance (public, English)

s08.question: Which drugs in our label set carry a boxed warning for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and what drug class are they?
s08.why: The warning is repeated across six separate labels; plain search fills its top five with versions of one or two labels, while one graph query lists all six cited drugs and their class.

gold.answer: Six drugs: abrocitinib, baricitinib, ritlecitinib, ruxolitinib, tofacitinib (including the extended-release tablets) and upadacitinib. The labels class five of them as Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors; the graph holds no class edge for ritlecitinib.

statements.label: Boxed warning (MACE) ← every drug whose label carries it
statements.gql: MATCH (w:`AdverseReaction`)<-[:`boxedWarning`]-(d:`Drug`) WHERE LOWER(w.name) CONTAINS 'major adverse cardiovascular' RETURN DISTINCT d.name AS drug ORDER BY drug LIMIT 30

statements.label: Same drugs → the drug class their labels state
statements.gql: MATCH (w:`AdverseReaction`)<-[:`boxedWarning`]-(d:`Drug`)-[:`inClass`]->(c:`DrugClass`) WHERE LOWER(w.name) CONTAINS 'major adverse cardiovascular' RETURN DISTINCT d.name AS drug, c.name AS drugClass ORDER BY drug LIMIT 30

s08.question: Which drugs are CYP3A4 substrates whose labels warn about strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and which CYP3A inhibitors do the labels name?
s08.why: Substrate status and the inhibitor warning sit in different sections of seven labels; the graph intersects both edges across the whole set and names the inhibitors, where plain search returns a few interaction paragraphs.

gold.answer: Seven substrates warn about strong CYP3A4 inhibitors: Kerendia (finerenone), apixaban, fentanyl, hydrocodone, oxycodone, ruxolitinib and tofacitinib. The labels name clarithromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole and ritonavir (strong inhibitors), plus amiodarone, dronedarone and fluconazole, as CYP3A inhibitors.

statements.label: Drug → substrate of CYP3A4, and the same drug → interacts with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
statements.gql: MATCH (d:`Drug`)-[:`substrateOf`]->(e:`Enzyme`), (d)-[:`interactsWithClass`]->(c:`DrugClass`) WHERE LOWER(e.name) CONTAINS 'cyp3a' AND LOWER(c.name) CONTAINS 'cyp3a4 inhibitor' AND NOT LOWER(c.name) CONTAINS 'moderate' RETURN DISTINCT d.name AS drug ORDER BY drug LIMIT 30

statements.label: Drugs the labels name as CYP3A inhibitors
statements.gql: MATCH (i:`Drug`)-[:`inhibitsEnzyme`]->(e:`Enzyme`) WHERE LOWER(e.name) CONTAINS 'cyp3a' RETURN DISTINCT i.name AS inhibitor ORDER BY inhibitor LIMIT 30

s08.question: Which adalimumab biosimilars are in our label set, and which company labels each one?
s08.why: Each biosimilar has its own label with near-identical text, so plain search returns a few lookalike passages; the graph returns every biosimilar with its labeler, each row cited to its own label.

gold.answer: Seven biosimilars, each with its own label: adalimumab-aacf (Fresenius Kabi), adalimumab-adaz (Sandoz; also Cordavis), adalimumab-adbm (Boehringer Ingelheim), adalimumab-afzb (Pfizer), adalimumab-aqvh (YUSIMRY, Meitheal), adalimumab-atto (Amgen) and adalimumab-ryvk (Teva).

statements.label: Every adalimumab biosimilar (FDA four-letter suffix) → labeled by company
statements.gql: MATCH (b:`Drug`)-[:`labeledBy`]->(c:`Company`) WHERE LOWER(b.name) CONTAINS 'adalimumab-' RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS biosimilar, c.name AS labeler ORDER BY biosimilar LIMIT 30

s08.question: Our bleeding protocol says idarucizumab (Praxbind) reverses apixaban. Which label supports that?
s08.why: Plain search returns reversal passages that mention both agents and leaves the reader to spot the mix-up; the graph shows idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran, proves no apixaban path exists and names the correct agent.

gold.answer: None. The premise is false. The idarucizumab label names dabigatran as the drug it reverses, and no idarucizumab → apixaban link exists. The andexanet alfa label is the one that names apixaban (and rivaroxaban).

statements.label: Premise check: what idarucizumab reverses
statements.gql: MATCH (d:`Drug`)-[:`reversedBy`]->(r:`Drug`) WHERE LOWER(r.name) CONTAINS 'idarucizumab' RETURN DISTINCT d.name AS reverses, r.name AS agent LIMIT 10

statements.label: Any apixaban → idarucizumab reversal link (expected: none)
statements.gql: MATCH (d:`Drug`)-[:`reversedBy`]->(r:`Drug`) WHERE LOWER(d.name) CONTAINS 'apixaban' AND LOWER(r.name) CONTAINS 'idarucizumab' RETURN d.name AS anticoagulant, r.name AS agent LIMIT 5

statements.label: Every anticoagulant → reversal agent pairing in the labels
statements.gql: MATCH (d:`Drug`)-[:`reversedBy`]->(r:`Drug`) RETURN DISTINCT d.name AS anticoagulant, r.name AS reversalAgent ORDER BY anticoagulant LIMIT 20

s09.why: The Topic Graph answers the corpus-wide question with named themes and their share of passages; plain search can only return five passages and cannot measure coverage.

gold.answer: The largest themes are opioid labeling (about 11% of passages), TNF blockers (7%), immune checkpoint inhibitors (6%), statins (6%), GLP-1 and insulin products (5%) and oral factor Xa anticoagulants (5%), followed by single-drug label themes and several ICD-10-CM coding-guideline themes of about 1-2% each.

s09.question: What is in this healthcare knowledge base?
s09.why: Plain hybrid search fills all five slots with ICD-10-CM coding passages from 2 areas; topic-balanced retrieval spreads them across 5 areas, adding oxycodone, Kerendia and sotalol labels.

gold.answer: A representative answer mixes the two halves of the collection: drug labels (for example oxycodone, Kerendia and sotalol) and ICD-10-CM coding rules and guidelines.

s09.question: Brief me on medication safety
s09.why: Plain hybrid search covers 4 areas, two of them anticoagulant labels; topic-balanced retrieval covers 5, adding GLP-1 and SGLT2-inhibitor labels.

gold.answer: A medication-safety briefing spans several drug classes: GLP-1 agonists (Ozempic), SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin and empagliflozin), insulin (Lantus) and oral factor Xa anticoagulants, including edoxaban (Savaysa).

manufacturing.title: Manufacturing: OSHA machine safety, severe-injury reports and NIST OT security (public, English)

s08.question: Which industries reported severe injuries involving industrial robots from 2015 through 2023?
s08.why: Each robot injury is its own report; plain search returns five of them, while one graph query returns all eighteen 2015-2023 reports with their industries, each cited.

gold.answer: Eighteen severe-injury reports from 2015-2023 involve robots. Automotive parts and motor-vehicle stamping lead with six; the rest span machinery makers (cooking appliances, HVAC and refrigeration equipment, lighting fixtures, lawn equipment, conveyors), metal fabrication and die-casting, a cheese plant, a sanitary-paper mill, ready-mix concrete, a broom maker and other manufacturing.

statements.label: Robot ← injury report → industry (2015-2023)
statements.gql: MATCH (e:`Equipment`)<-[:`reportEquipment`]-(i:`InjuryReport`)-[:`reportIndustry`]->(n:`Industry`) WHERE LOWER(e.name) CONTAINS 'robot' AND NOT i.name CONTAINS ' 2024' AND NOT i.name CONTAINS ' 2025' RETURN DISTINCT i.name AS report, n.name AS industry ORDER BY report LIMIT 60

s08.question: Which industrial-robot injuries from 2015 through 2023 happened while machinery was being maintained or cleaned, and which OSHA standard requires the control for that hazard?
s08.why: The injury reports describe the incidents and OSHA's booklets name the standard; the graph joins each robot report's hazard to lockout/tagout and 29 CFR 1910.147, with citations on both sides.

gold.answer: Ten of the eighteen robot injuries happened during maintenance or cleaning (reports 2015-041979, 2016-010111, 2016-1110325, 2018-066216, 2018-076656, 2019-0910191, 2021-031862, 2021-108852, 2022-021585 and 2023-032373). That hazard is controlled by lockout/tagout, which 29 CFR 1910.147 requires.

statements.label: Robot ← injury report → maintenance or cleaning hazard (2015-2023)
statements.gql: MATCH (e:`Equipment`)<-[:`reportEquipment`]-(i:`InjuryReport`)-[:`reportHazard`]->(h:`Hazard`) WHERE LOWER(e.name) CONTAINS 'robot' AND LOWER(h.name) CONTAINS 'maintenance' AND NOT i.name CONTAINS ' 2024' AND NOT i.name CONTAINS ' 2025' RETURN DISTINCT i.name AS report, h.name AS hazard ORDER BY report LIMIT 20

statements.label: That hazard → controlled by lockout/tagout ← standard that requires it
statements.gql: MATCH (s:`Standard`)-[:`standardRequiresControl`]->(k:`Control`)<-[:`hazardControlledBy`]-(h:`Hazard`) WHERE k.name = 'lockout/tagout' AND LOWER(h.name) CONTAINS 'maintenance, cleaning' RETURN DISTINCT h.name AS hazard, k.name AS control, s.name AS standard LIMIT 10

s08.question: Which cyber threats and real-world incidents involving PLCs and SCADA systems do the NIST OT security guides describe?
s08.why: The incidents are scattered across sections and appendices of two revisions of NIST SP 800-82; plain search returns a few of those passages, while one graph query returns every system → threat pair with its citation.

gold.answer: Named incidents include the Unitronics Vision Series PLC defacement campaign (via default credentials and malicious projects), Stuxnet against SCADA systems, the AcidRain destructive attack on automated SCADA controls and remote access to the SCADA computer for the Bowman Dam. The guides also tie PLCs and SCADA to malware, manipulation of control and excessive network traffic.

statements.label: PLC or SCADA system → exposed to threat or incident
statements.gql: MATCH (s:`OTSystem`)-[:`systemExposedTo`]->(r:`CyberRisk`) WHERE LOWER(s.name) CONTAINS 'plc' OR LOWER(s.name) CONTAINS 'scada' RETURN DISTINCT s.name AS system, r.name AS threat ORDER BY system LIMIT 30

s08.question: Our press brakes fall under OSHA's mechanical power press standard, 29 CFR 1910.217, so we need its PSDI certification for them, right?
s08.why: Plain search returns press passages that discuss presses and press brakes side by side; the graph shows what 1910.217 covers, proves no link to press brakes exists and names the standard that does apply.

gold.answer: No. 29 CFR 1910.217 covers mechanical power presses, and its paragraph (a)(5) explicitly excludes press brakes. The graph has no 1910.217 → press brake link; OSHA's safeguarding guide points press brakes to ANSI B11.3 (Safety Requirements for Power Press Brakes) instead.

statements.label: Premise check: what 29 CFR 1910.217 covers
statements.gql: MATCH (s:`Standard`)-[:`standardCoversEquipment`]->(e:`Equipment`) WHERE s.name CONTAINS '1910.217' RETURN DISTINCT s.name AS standard, e.name AS covers ORDER BY standard LIMIT 20

statements.label: Any 1910.217 → press brake coverage (expected: none)
statements.gql: MATCH (s:`Standard`)-[:`standardCoversEquipment`]->(e:`Equipment`) WHERE s.name CONTAINS '1910.217' AND LOWER(e.name) CONTAINS 'brake' RETURN s.name AS standard, e.name AS equipment LIMIT 5

statements.label: What does cover press brakes
statements.gql: MATCH (s:`Standard`)-[:`standardCoversEquipment`]->(e:`Equipment`) WHERE LOWER(e.name) CONTAINS 'press brake' RETURN DISTINCT s.name AS standard, e.name AS equipment LIMIT 10

s09.question: What are the main themes across this manufacturing safety and OT security collection, and how much of it does each cover?
s09.why: The Topic Graph answers the corpus-wide question with named themes and their share of passages; plain search can only return five passages and cannot measure coverage.

gold.answer: About half is operational technology security (nine themes, from OT and IoT security at about 11% of passages to OT security controls, manufacturing cyber risk and OT asset monitoring). About 39% is physical machine safety: two finger-amputation themes (12% and 11%), machine safeguarding and energy control (8%), PSDI press certification (4%) and powered industrial trucks (4%). Manufacturing standards and evaluation methods make up about 9%.

s09.question: Break down the machine safeguarding and energy control content: which sub-themes does it contain and how large is each?
s09.why: The Topic Graph already knows how the safeguarding content splits and in what proportion; plain search returns safeguarding passages without grouping or measuring them.

gold.answer: About 8% of passages, split into OSHA lockout/tagout and machine safety, lockout/tagout energy control, and machine guards and safeguarding devices (about 2% each), plus mechanical power press safety, safeguarding food equipment and the machine amputation hazards guide (about 1% each).

s09.question: What should a new plant safety manager know?
s09.why: Plain hybrid search draws its five passages from 3 areas, mostly lockout/tagout; topic-balanced retrieval spreads them across 5, adding OT security, production-system standards and burn injuries.

gold.answer: A useful briefing spans lockout/tagout, OT configuration risks and cybersecurity governance, production-system standards and chemical and thermal burn injuries.

s09.question: What should a maintenance technician know before servicing equipment?
s09.why: Plain hybrid search returns five lockout/tagout passages from a single area; topic-balanced retrieval spreads them across 4, adding press safety, OT cybersecurity controls and incident response.

gold.answer: Lockout/tagout procedures, mechanical power press safety, and the cybersecurity controls and incident response for the systems being serviced.

energy.title: Energy: U.S. grid reliability, FERC orders, DOE OE-417 events and EIA analysis (public domain, English)

s08.question: Which cyber events did utilities report to DOE on form OE-417 from 2019 through 2024?
s08.why: Each OE-417 record is its own document; plain search returns five cyber events, while one graph query returns all twenty-two from 2019-2024, each cited to its record.

gold.answer: Twenty-two cyber events, all from 2020-2024 (none in 2019): three in 2020, five in 2021, five in 2022, four in 2023 and five in 2024. They span Texas, Florida, the Northeast, the Midwest and the West, and include operational-technology events in Cleveland County, North Carolina (January 2024) and Washington County, Minnesota (March 2024).

statements.label: Grid event → cause: cyber (2019-2024)

s08.question: What caused the Odessa, Texas inverter disturbances, how did FERC respond, and which ride-through standards were finally approved?
s08.why: Plain search finds the right Federal Register orders, but the reader still has to stitch the causes, FERC's response, the 2025 approval and the version chain together from five passages; the graph returns each hop as cited rows.

gold.answer: The first two Odessa events (2021) were caused by inverter-based resources tripping or entering momentary cessation; the third followed a normally cleared single-line-to-ground fault. FERC responded with an order directing registration of inverter-based resources and Order No. 901 (Reliability Standards to Address Inverter-Based Resources). In 2025, Order No. 909 approved PRC-029-1 and PRC-024-4. PRC-024-4 supersedes PRC-024-3, which superseded PRC-024-2.

statements.label: Odessa event → cause
statements.gql: MATCH (ev:`GridEvent`)-[:`eventCause`]->(c:`Cause`) WHERE LOWER(ev.name) CONTAINS 'odessa' RETURN DISTINCT ev.name AS event, c.name AS cause LIMIT 20

statements.label: FERC order → responds to the Odessa disturbances
statements.gql: MATCH (o:`Order`)-[:`orderRespondsTo`]->(ev:`GridEvent`) WHERE LOWER(ev.name) CONTAINS 'odessa' RETURN DISTINCT o.name AS order, ev.name AS event LIMIT 10

statements.label: Order No. 909 → approves ride-through standards
statements.gql: MATCH (o:`Order`)-[:`orderApproves`]->(s:`ReliabilityStandard`) WHERE o.name = 'Order No. 909' RETURN DISTINCT o.name AS order, s.name AS standard LIMIT 10

statements.label: PRC-024 version chain
statements.gql: MATCH (n:`ReliabilityStandard`)-[:`supersedes`]->(o:`ReliabilityStandard`) WHERE n.name CONTAINS 'PRC-024' RETURN DISTINCT n.name AS newer, o.name AS older LIMIT 10

s08.question: What caused the energy disruptions in Winter Storm Uri (2021) and Winter Storm Elliott (2022), according to EIA and FERC?
s08.why: The causes are spread across a dozen EIA articles, FERC's winter assessment and Federal Register orders; plain search returns five passages about one storm, while the graph lists each storm's cited causes side by side.

gold.answer: Both combined extreme cold with natural-gas supply problems, notably freeze-offs of wells and pipes. Uri (February 2021) is tied to extreme cold, a cold snap, natural-gas fuel issues and weather-related production problems. Elliott (December 2022) is tied to extremely cold temperatures, high winds and blizzards, freeze-offs, pipeline constraints and limited pipeline capacity, and scheduling mismatches.

statements.label: Winter Storm Uri (February 2021) → causes
statements.gql: MATCH (ev:`GridEvent`)-[:`eventCause`]->(c:`Cause`) WHERE LOWER(ev.name) CONTAINS 'winter storm uri' OR LOWER(ev.name) CONTAINS 'february 2021' RETURN DISTINCT ev.name AS event, c.name AS cause ORDER BY event LIMIT 40

statements.label: Winter Storm Elliott (December 2022) → causes
statements.gql: MATCH (ev:`GridEvent`)-[:`eventCause`]->(c:`Cause`) WHERE LOWER(ev.name) CONTAINS 'elliott' RETURN DISTINCT ev.name AS event, c.name AS cause ORDER BY event LIMIT 40

s08.question: EOP-012-1 is still the current extreme cold weather standard for generators, right?
s08.why: Plain search surfaces EOP-012-1 passages that read as current; the graph follows the supersedes chain to EOP-012-3, proves nothing newer exists in the corpus and cites the approving order.

gold.answer: No. EOP-012-2 superseded EOP-012-1, and EOP-012-3 superseded EOP-012-2. Nothing in these documents supersedes EOP-012-3, which FERC approved in 2025 (192 FERC ¶ 61,229, which also directed data collection).

statements.label: Premise check: EOP-012 version chain
statements.gql: MATCH (n:`ReliabilityStandard`)-[:`supersedes`]->(o:`ReliabilityStandard`) WHERE n.name CONTAINS 'EOP-012' RETURN DISTINCT n.name AS newer, o.name AS older ORDER BY newer LIMIT 10

statements.label: Anything that supersedes EOP-012-3 (expected: none)
statements.gql: MATCH (n:`ReliabilityStandard`)-[:`supersedes`]->(o:`ReliabilityStandard`) WHERE o.name CONTAINS 'EOP-012-3' RETURN n.name AS newer, o.name AS older LIMIT 5

statements.label: Order that approved EOP-012-3
statements.gql: MATCH (o:`Order`)-[:`orderApproves`]->(s:`ReliabilityStandard`) WHERE s.name = 'EOP-012-3' AND o.name CONTAINS '192 FERC' RETURN DISTINCT o.name AS order, s.name AS standard LIMIT 5

s09.question: What are the main themes across this grid reliability collection, and how much of it does each cover?
s09.why: The Topic Graph answers the corpus-wide question with named themes and their share of passages; plain search can only return five passages and cannot measure coverage.

gold.answer: DOE OE-417 event records (about 12% of passages), seasonal reliability and capacity (12%), smart grid distribution automation (9%), the U.S. energy and economic outlook (9%), extreme cold weather standards (9%) and NERC standards citations (8%), followed by inverter-based resource standards and modeling, 2018 grid disturbances, extreme heat and cold planning, network security monitoring, demand response, EOP-012 burden analysis and interruption metrics.

s09.question: Break down the DOE OE-417 event records: which kinds of events are there and how large is each group?
s09.why: The Topic Graph already knows how the OE-417 records split by event type and in what proportion; plain search returns individual event records without grouping or measuring them.

gold.answer: About 12% of passages, split into system operations events, Texas severe-weather events, severe-weather outages and physical attacks (about 2% each), plus 2024 cyber events, 2024 generator losses, fuel supply events and California severe-weather impacts (about 1% each).

s09.question: What is in this energy knowledge base?
s09.why: Plain hybrid search draws its five passages from 2 areas, three of them from one EIA outlook; topic-balanced retrieval spreads them across 5.

gold.answer: A representative answer samples inverter-based resource standards and ride-through rules, distribution automation results, EIA's regional generation outlook and NERC's winter reliability assessment.

s09.why: Plain hybrid search draws its five passages from 2 areas; topic-balanced retrieval spreads them across 4, adding inverter-based resource standards and generator cold-weather constraints.
